paragraphs: A graphon represents the underlying structure of dense networks as a continuous function. Estimating one can become expensive when a method must infer hidden node variables or solve difficult graph comparison problems. This paper instead learns from counts of small subgraph patterns, treating these counts as summary statistics that the estimated graphon should reproduce.

The estimator uses an implicit neural representation: a network maps coordinates directly to graphon values. Training matches the observed pattern counts without explicitly modeling latent node variables. This provides a polynomial-time approach and avoids the combinatorial optimization associated with Gromov–Wasserstein comparisons. The authors also introduce MomentMixup, which augments data by mixing these summary statistics.

The theoretical guarantee is conditional: observed motifs must sufficiently represent those of the true graphon, as can occur with sufficiently large or numerous graph samples. Under that condition, the authors bound estimation error in cut distance. Empirically, their estimator beats scalable competitors in 75% of benchmark settings and matches them elsewhere; MomentMixup improves classification on most benchmarks.
neurips-2025-a-few-moments-please-scalab.tldr: Matching subgraph counts lets a neural graphon estimator avoid costly graph comparisons while providing conditional error guarantees and strong benchmark results.

paragraphs: Small translations of an image can change a vision transformer's output even when its content remains the same. Convolutional networks also have imperfect shift invariance because downsampling and nonlinear operations can introduce aliasing. This paper builds on approaches that address those sources of instability and brings that reasoning into the design of a vision transformer.

Alias-Free ViT combines alias-free downsampling and nonlinearities with linear cross-covariance attention. The attention mechanism is shift-equivariant for both whole-pixel and fractional translations: its representation follows the image's movement in a consistent way. This supports a global representation that remains invariant to those shifts, connecting the behavior of internal features to the desired stability of the final representation.

The reported experiments show competitive image classification performance and better robustness to adversarial translations than similarly sized models. The contribution therefore concerns both architectural behavior and measured robustness. It shows how addressing translation sensitivity within the model's operations can preserve classification capability while making deliberately chosen image shifts less disruptive in the evaluated comparisons.
neurips-2025-alias-free-vit-fractional-s.tldr: Alias-Free ViT combines alias-free operations with shift-equivariant attention to improve robustness to image translations while maintaining competitive classification performance.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input belongs to classes a model is intended to recognize. Pretrained vision-language models have worked well for this task, but their effectiveness has lacked a formal explanation. This paper analyzes CLIP-based detectors through point-wise mutual information, a quantity describing the association between a particular image and an in-distribution label.

The authors show that existing post-hoc methods effectively estimate this quantity stochastically and use it to construct energy functions representing the in-distribution data. This interpretation turns detector design into an estimation problem. Their proposed method applies the chain rule of point-wise mutual information to divide that problem into several easier estimation tasks.

The decomposition reduces estimation complexity and provably raises the estimation upper bound, with the aim of reducing underestimation bias. These theoretical results explain the motivation for changing how the association is estimated. Across mainstream benchmarks, the resulting method achieves reported state-of-the-art performance in multiple detection setups, connecting the information-theoretic analysis to empirical improvements in identifying unknown classes.
neurips-2025-an-information-theoretical-.tldr: An information-theoretic analysis of CLIP-based detection motivates decomposing image–label association estimates, improving out-of-distribution detection across evaluated setups.

paragraphs: Estimating what would happen under a treatment is more useful when accompanied by uncertainty intervals. This is especially relevant when treatment varies continuously, such as an amount or dose, rather than taking only a few discrete values. The paper extends conformal prediction to potential outcomes under continuous treatments, addressing a setting not covered by the existing methods described in the abstract.

A central issue is that treatment assignment information, represented by the propensity score, is often unknown and must be learned from data. Treating that estimate as exact would overlook an additional source of uncertainty. The proposed approach explicitly accounts for propensity estimation when constructing intervals, allowing validity even when the true propensity score is unavailable.

The authors derive finite-sample validity guarantees and provide an algorithm for computing the resulting intervals. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate their effectiveness. The contribution combines a theoretical extension with a usable calculation procedure: uncertainty about treatment assignment becomes part of interval construction rather than requiring the assignment mechanism to be known beforehand.
neurips-2025-conformal-prediction-for-ca.tldr: The paper develops conformal intervals for continuous-treatment potential outcomes that account for uncertainty in estimated propensity scores.

paragraphs: In a constrained multi-armed bandit problem, a learner must discover good actions while respecting restrictions. Standard regret bounds describe worst-case learning costs, but they may obscure easier instances. This paper asks whether bounds can instead adapt to the actual loss sequence while still accounting for constraints, potentially providing smaller guarantees when the instance permits them.

The authors answer this question for adversarial losses and stochastic constraints. Their main setting uses hard constraints, requiring them to hold throughout learning with high probability. The proposed algorithm has a regret bound with two data-dependent components: one measures the difficulty of satisfying constraints, and the other measures the learning difficulty independently of those constraints.

A matching structural lower-bound result shows that both components reflect fundamental aspects of the problem rather than merely weaknesses of this algorithm's analysis. This separation explains why constrained learning can remain difficult for two distinct reasons. The work also develops results for soft constraints, extending the analysis to a related setting where the restrictions are less demanding.
neurips-2025-data-dependent-regret-bound.tldr: Data-dependent regret bounds separate the inherent costs of learning and satisfying constraints in bandits with adversarial losses and stochastic constraints.

paragraphs: Stereo depth systems can become dangerous when they interpret nearby objects as distant. Adversarial patches provide a way to expose such weaknesses before deployment. This paper examines why repeated textures that mislead depth models digitally can lose effectiveness when implemented as physical patches, making them less useful for testing real systems.

The authors find that the arrangement of repeated textures matters substantially. Introducing regular spaces between them creates a grid structure that improves attack performance. They investigate how variations in this structure affect the attack, then develop a method that jointly optimizes the spacing structure and the texture elements. The contribution makes spatial organization an explicit part of patch design.

The resulting patches successfully attack RAFT-Stereo and STTR, which represent different stereo estimation approaches. The authors also report attacks on Intel RealSense RGB-D cameras under real-world conditions. These findings connect the structural observation to practical vulnerability assessment: physical performance depends on more than repeating an optimized texture, and commercial depth sensing can also exhibit the tested weakness.
neurips-2025-depthvanish-optimizing-adve.tldr: DepthVanish jointly optimizes texture and spacing in adversarial patches, demonstrating attacks on stereo models and physical Intel RealSense cameras.

paragraphs: As generated writing becomes more similar to human writing, detectors face increasingly overlapping text features. DNA-DetectLLM approaches detection through a repair process inspired by DNA. Its central idea is to measure the work involved in changing a passage toward an ideal AI-generated sequence, producing a detection signal tied to explicit modifications of the input.

For each input, the method constructs that idealized sequence and repeatedly repairs tokens judged non-optimal. It accumulates the repair effort and uses the total to distinguish human-written from AI-generated text. This makes the signal interpretable in terms of the repair procedure. The authors present the approach as zero-shot detection, with the mutation-repair perspective organizing how each text is assessed.

Across multiple public benchmarks, the paper reports state-of-the-art detection results, including relative improvements of 5.55% in AUROC and 2.08% in F1. It also reports strong robustness across tested adversarial attacks and input lengths. These findings support repair effort as a useful empirical discriminator when the feature distributions of human and generated text substantially overlap.
neurips-2025-dna-detectllm-unveiling-ai-.tldr: DNA-DetectLLM detects AI-generated text using cumulative token-repair effort, with reported improvements in detection and robustness on public benchmarks.

paragraphs: Modeling a drug bound to its target requires accounting for how the target's shape can change during binding. Approaches based only on rigid transformations can miss these adaptations, particularly when the conformational change is substantial. DynaPhArM addresses this problem with an atom-level model designed to represent drug-specific changes in target–drug complexes.

The method uses an SE(3)-equivariant transformer, whose geometric behavior respects rotations and translations. Cooperative scalar-vector representations, drug-specific embeddings, and a diffusion process model the evolving interactions. A multi-task learning framework additionally incorporates physical and energetic information, including bond lengths, bond angles, and van der Waals interactions. These components connect flexible structural modeling with constraints that preserve essential molecular geometry.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance, an overall RMSD of 2.01 Å, a sc-RMSD of 0.29 Å, and higher success rates than existing methods. They also describe promise for improving drug specificity through modeling how targets adapt to different drugs. That prospective value rests on the demonstrated ability to represent atomic interactions and conformational flexibility.
neurips-2025-dynapharm-adaptive-and-phys.tldr: DynaPhArM combines equivariant modeling, diffusion, and physical constraints to capture drug-specific conformational changes in target–drug complexes.

paragraphs: Forecasting complex dynamics requires representing both temporal dependence and uncertainty that grows further into the future. Predicting each future state individually can miss those relationships. Elucidated Rolling Diffusion Models combine a rolling forecast structure, which assigns more noise to longer forecast horizons, with the high-fidelity diffusion design of Elucidated Diffusion Models.

The authors adapt the noise schedule, network preconditioning, and Heun sampler to this rolling setting. A new loss weighting scheme emphasizes intermediate horizons, where relatively predictable behavior gives way to greater uncertainty. A pretrained diffusion model initializes the first window, while a hybrid sequence architecture extracts spatial and temporal features as the forecast is progressively denoised.

On two-dimensional Navier–Stokes simulations and ERA5 global weather forecasting at 1.5-degree resolution, the method consistently outperforms the key diffusion baselines evaluated, including conditional autoregressive EDM. These results support integrating forecast structure and diffusion design when uncertainty propagation matters. The method's distinctive emphasis is on how predictions across time are represented and refined together within the forecasting process.
neurips-2025-elucidated-rolling-diffusio.tldr: ERDM adapts high-fidelity diffusion modeling to rolling forecasts, improving evaluated fluid and weather predictions while explicitly representing growing uncertainty.

paragraphs: Endoscopy requires several kinds of visual and clinical understanding, so a benchmark focused on a narrow task can give an incomplete picture of model capability. EndoBench evaluates multimodal language models across a broader range of endoscopic practice. Its organization follows clinical activities, including anatomical recognition, lesion analysis, spatial localization, and surgical operations.

The benchmark contains 6,832 validated visual question-answer pairs drawn from 21 datasets. It spans four endoscopic scenarios, 12 specialized tasks with 12 secondary subtasks, and five levels of visual prompting granularity. The authors evaluate 23 models covering general-purpose, medical-specialized, and proprietary systems, and include clinician performance as a reference. This breadth allows model performance to be examined across different tasks and presentation formats.

Proprietary models perform best overall among the evaluated model categories but remain behind human experts. Medical-domain supervised fine-tuning substantially improves task-specific accuracy, while prompt format and task complexity continue to affect results. Together, these findings show both measurable progress and a persistent gap between current model performance and expert clinical reasoning.
neurips-2025-endobench-a-comprehensive-e.tldr: EndoBench evaluates 23 multimodal models across diverse endoscopy tasks and finds substantial variation by model, task, and prompting, with experts still ahead.

paragraphs: Language models sometimes reject harmless requests because their wording resembles unsafe content. EVOREFUSE generates these pseudo-malicious instructions to evaluate and reduce unnecessary refusals. It addresses the difficulty of collecting examples that are simultaneously diverse, scalable to produce, and effective at exposing overly conservative model behavior.

The method evolves seed instructions using mutations and recombination. Its optimization objective increases a lower bound on refusal probability, guiding the search toward prompts that elicit confident refusals. The authors create EVOREFUSE-TEST with 582 instructions and EVOREFUSE-ALIGN with 3,000 instruction-response examples for supervised and preference-based alignment. The evaluation set improves refusal triggering, lexical diversity, and response confidence over the next-best benchmark in the reported comparisons.

Supervised fine-tuning of LLAMA3.1-8B-INSTRUCT on the alignment set reduces over-refusals by up to 29.85% relative to training on the second-best alignment dataset, without compromising safety in the reported evaluation. Analysis suggests that models can overemphasize sensitive keywords while overlooking broader context. The work connects that observed failure pattern to both evaluation data and corrective training.
neurips-2025-evorefuse-evolutionary-prom.tldr: EVOREFUSE evolves harmless refusal-triggering prompts into evaluation and alignment datasets, helping reduce measured over-refusal without sacrificing evaluated safety.

paragraphs: Face recognition needs information that distinguishes identities, but facial representations can also retain visual clues that help reconstruct a person's appearance. FracFace aims to weaken those reconstruction clues while preserving the information needed for recognition. Its approach modifies frequency-domain features and their spatial organization to make recovering facial appearance more difficult.

The framework first applies a Frequency Channels Refining module, which reduces sparsity in frequency-domain features. This stage suppresses reconstruction-relevant clues while preserving features useful for recognizing identity. A Frequency Fractal Mapping module then remaps the refined channels into a fractal-based structure. The authors use the self-similarity of fractals to retain identity-related information while further obscuring the deep representation.

Experiments on multiple public face recognition benchmarks show substantially reduced visual recoverability alongside high recognition accuracy. The authors also report advantages over state-of-the-art privacy protection approaches. The result supports a practical separation between recognizing someone and recovering their appearance: the representation remains useful for the former while making the tested reconstruction attacks more challenging.
neurips-2025-fracface-breaking-the-visua.tldr: FracFace refines and fractally remaps frequency features to reduce facial reconstruction while maintaining high recognition accuracy on evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: An exploring agent can become trapped in a representational feedback loop: its autoencoder emphasizes frequently visited states, and the agent then samples goals from that same representation. In visual environments, this can restrict which behaviors it learns. DRAG addresses this problem by encouraging the learned representation to cover a broader portion of the environment's state space.

The method combines a beta-VAE with distributionally robust optimization. An adversarial neural network reweights the states used to train the autoencoder, accounting for the mismatch between the agent's current experience and unseen parts of the environment. Training progressively encourages a shift toward a uniform state distribution, so common observations do not dominate the representation as strongly.

The authors report improved state coverage and downstream control in difficult exploration environments, including mazes and robotic tasks requiring movement around walls. These improvements occur without pretraining or prior environment knowledge. The findings support treating representation learning as part of exploration itself: how experience is weighted influences which goals become available and which skills the agent learns.
neurips-2025-imagine-beyond-distribution.tldr: DRAG reweights autoencoder training to broaden learned state representations, improving exploration and control without pretraining or prior environment knowledge.

paragraphs: A bandit learner chooses actions while observing only limited feedback, and delayed observations make those choices harder. This paper studies delays chosen adversarially while seeking one algorithm that performs well under either stochastic or adversarial outcomes. This best-of-both-worlds goal requires adapting to easier statistical structure without losing protection against difficult outcome sequences.

In the adversarial regime, the proposed algorithm achieves regret scaling with the square root of the number of arms times the number of rounds, plus the square root of cumulative delay, up to logarithmic factors. In the stochastic regime, its bound depends on the gaps between arms and on the maximum number of observations still missing.

The algorithm matches known lower bounds in both regimes up to logarithmic factors. Its stochastic delay contribution improves the previous best result by a factor equal to the number of arms. The advance is therefore both simultaneous and regime-specific: one algorithm achieves strong guarantees across environments, while its stochastic guarantee also improves what was known even outside the best-of-both-worlds requirement.
neurips-2025-improved-best-of-both-world.tldr: A new delayed-feedback bandit algorithm matches known stochastic and adversarial regret lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: Longer reasoning can improve a model's answers, but it can also produce redundant steps that consume computation without helping the solution. Self-Braking Tuning trains reasoning models to regulate when they stop. The approach focuses on learning this behavior within the model, reducing dependence on external mechanisms that intervene during generation.

The authors define overthinking metrics using standard answers and use them to identify unnecessary parts of reasoning trajectories. Those detections become training signals for self-regulation. They then construct training data with adaptive reasoning lengths and introduce a braking prompt mechanism, giving the model examples of when its reasoning should terminate.

Experiments on AIME, AMC, MATH500, and GSM8K report token reductions of up to 60% while maintaining accuracy comparable to unconstrained models. The result supports teaching stopping behavior as a component of reasoning ability. The maximum reported saving describes the evaluated outcomes; the broader finding is that learning to recognize redundant reasoning can reduce generation cost while preserving comparable mathematical task performance.
neurips-2025-let-lrms-break-free-from-ov.tldr: Self-Braking Tuning teaches reasoning models when to stop, cutting token use by up to 60% with comparable accuracy on evaluated math benchmarks.

paragraphs: Matching the same person across visible-light and infrared images is difficult without costly identity annotations. Unsupervised methods replace those labels with clusters and cross-modality matches, but errors in these pseudo-labels can limit learning. This paper uses attributes extracted by a large vision-language model to improve both labeling and the representations used for matching.

Its attribute-aware labeling strategy refines clusters within each modality using image-level attributes. It then groups clusters using cluster-level attributes to improve matching between modalities. An explicit-implicit attribute fusion module produces more detailed identity-related text features, and an attribute-aware contrastive module uses static and dynamic text features to encourage representations that remain consistent across visible and infrared imagery.

Experiments on person re-identification datasets support the effectiveness of the overall approach and its individual components. The method significantly outperforms existing unsupervised methods and surpasses several supervised methods in the reported evaluations. The findings suggest that semantic attributes can improve the reliability of automatically generated supervision while also helping bridge differences between the two image modalities.
neurips-2025-lvlm-driven-attribute-aware.tldr: Vision-language attributes improve pseudo-labels and cross-modality representations for unsupervised visible–infrared person matching.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model for one task can degrade its performance on other tasks. This paper investigates why training with model-generated data can reduce that degradation compared with using ground-truth data. Its analysis connects preservation of non-target performance to the token-level characteristics of the sequences used during fine-tuning.

The authors find that generated sequences contain fewer high-perplexity tokens, meaning tokens that are relatively surprising to the model. Their analysis identifies this reduction as the source of improved robustness on non-target tasks in the studied settings. They then test the explanation directly by masking high-perplexity tokens in ground-truth training data, achieving comparable preservation of non-target performance.

Experiments across different model families and sizes, including Gemma 2 IT 2B and Llama 3 8B Instruct, agree with this account. The practical implication is that the benefit associated with generated data can also be obtained through selective token learning. The paper provides an empirical explanation for mitigating forgetting, linking a measurable property of training tokens to cross-domain performance after fine-tuning.
neurips-2025-mitigating-forgetting-in-ll.tldr: Experiments link reduced forgetting during fine-tuning to fewer high-perplexity tokens, with token masking reproducing the preservation benefits of generated data.

paragraphs: Many decision-making systems operate in environments whose dynamics change over time. Non-stationary Markov decision processes describe these settings, but comparing algorithms is difficult without shared simulation tools. NS-Gym provides an open-source toolkit specifically for these changing environments, integrating with Gymnasium to support a more standardized experimental foundation.

The central design choice separates changes in environmental parameters from the agent's decision-making module. Researchers can therefore specify how an environment evolves as a distinct component of the simulation. The toolkit incorporates important characteristics and types of non-stationary problems, alongside interfaces and benchmark tasks intended to support consistent, reproducible evaluations.

The paper reviews prior work and uses NS-Gym to benchmark several existing algorithmic approaches. Its contribution is primarily infrastructure for studying adaptation: a common framework makes environmental change an explicit part of the problem specification. The authors envision it enabling broader research on decision-making under non-stationarity by giving researchers reusable simulations and a shared basis for comparing how algorithms respond to changing conditions.
neurips-2025-ns-gym-a-comprehensive-and-.tldr: NS-Gym supplies modular Gymnasium-based simulations and benchmarks for evaluating decision-making algorithms in environments that change over time.

paragraphs: Scientific solution fields can contain sharp transitions, fine oscillations, and localized structures. These high-frequency features are difficult for implicit neural representations to capture, particularly when one network must represent many fields. PDEfuncta addresses that shared-representation setting, extending attention beyond methods designed to fit only a single solution instance.

Its main component is Global Fourier Modulation, which injects high-frequency information into every network layer through Fourier-based reparameterization. This supports compact representations of multiple solution fields using low-dimensional latent vectors. The authors build a meta-learning framework around this mechanism to learn multi-modal solution fields and support generalization to new tasks.

Empirical studies across diverse scientific problems show improved representation quality. The paper also reports potential for forward and inverse inference without retraining, preserving a distinction between demonstrated representational improvements and the broader promise for inference tasks. The approach matters because it tackles fine-scale detail within a reusable shared network, connecting compact latent descriptions with the ability to represent complicated solution behavior.
neurips-2025-pdefuncta-spectrally-aware-.tldr: PDEfuncta uses Fourier modulation to improve shared neural representations of detailed PDE solution fields and shows promise for inference without retraining.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can require substantial memory and processing time, limiting their use on constrained devices. QSVD reduces these costs by combining low-rank approximation with low-precision computation. It focuses on the query, key, and value weight matrices used in attention, applying singular-value decomposition to them jointly.

A low-rank approximation represents the matrices with a smaller structure. QSVD dynamically allocates the retained rank according to its effect on model accuracy, making the compression decision sensitive to the consequences for task performance. The approach targets both computational overhead and key-value cache size. It also quantizes model weights and activations, combining two forms of compression within the same method.

The authors report more than 10% accuracy improvement over previous approaches relying only on quantization or SVD, alongside lower hardware cost. These comparisons support coordinating rank selection and numerical precision when compressing vision-language models. The proposed combination is intended to make real-time deployment more practical while preserving more task capability than the evaluated single-technique approaches.
neurips-2025-qsvd-efficient-low-rank-app.tldr: QSVD combines joint query–key–value low-rank compression, accuracy-aware rank allocation, and quantization to reduce vision-language model costs.

paragraphs: Efficient instruction tuning depends on choosing useful training data, but selecting whole sequences can overlook the different contributions of individual response tokens. Quadratic Coreset Selection combines sequence-level and token-level influence in a principled selection objective. This addresses both the value of important tokens and the potential effects of token noise and bias.

The original formulation faces a severe computational obstacle: it involves inverting Hessian matrices at language-model scale. The authors develop a probabilistic variant using reparameterized densities to relax that formulation. A solver based on hierarchical policy gradients learns this variant without requiring back-propagation. The paper establishes convergence and asymptotic equivalence to the original objective.

Experiments show improved sequence-level data efficiency and additional gains from using token-level influence strategically. The method succeeds in regular and targeted instruction tuning, including free-form complex instruction following and chain-of-thought reasoning. These findings connect the selection objective to practical post-training performance, showing how decisions about complete examples and their individual tokens can be considered within a shared framework.
neurips-2025-quadratic-coreset-selection.tldr: Quadratic Coreset Selection unifies sequence and token influence through a tractable probabilistic solver with theoretical guarantees and improved instruction-tuning efficiency.

paragraphs: Compressing a language model to very few bits introduces approximation errors whose effects depend on where they occur and which directions they take. RSAVQ addresses both issues within vector quantization. Its central idea is to use the model's sensitivity geometry to guide errors and distribute a limited bit budget.

Error Direction Sensitivity Guidance uses a Riemannian metric induced by the Fisher information matrix. It projects quantization errors toward low-sensitivity directions, specifically along the negative natural gradient direction, to suppress error expansion. Weight Channel Sensitivity Guidance uses curvature information from the same matrix to measure channel sensitivity and dynamically allocate bits. The authors describe this as facilitating a globally optimal quantization solution under prescribed bit constraints.

Experiments report improvements over existing methods. For two-bit LLaMA-3 8B quantization, RSAVQ leads baselines including VPTQ and QuIP# by 0.4 in perplexity and 1.5 in zero-shot accuracy. The results support considering error direction and channel sensitivity together when compressing models for resource-constrained environments.
neurips-2025-rsavq-riemannian-sensitivit.tldr: RSAVQ uses Fisher-information geometry to guide quantization errors and bit allocation, improving evaluated extremely low-bit language models.

paragraphs: Language-model unlearning aims to remove unwanted training-data influences while preserving useful abilities. Simply reversing learning through gradient ascent can allow uncontrolled deviation from the pretrained model. This paper revisits negative preference optimization, an approach developed to address that problem, and identifies a separate issue arising from its use of a reference model.

The authors call this issue reference model bias. Measuring unlearning relative to the original model can give a misleading impression of effectiveness for individual data points. It can allocate optimization effort unevenly across examples of different difficulty and make early gradient-weight smoothing ineffective. SimNPO removes reliance on that reference model through a simpler preference-optimization formulation.

The paper analyzes why this change can help, including through mixtures of Markov chains, and evaluates the method on TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP. The reported experiments support its effectiveness. The contribution links a specific source of optimization bias to a structural simplification, showing how the choice of comparison model can influence which unwanted data receives useful unlearning effort.
neurips-2025-simplicity-prevails-rethink.tldr: SimNPO removes the reference model from negative preference optimization to address biased allocation of unlearning effort.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples through a sequence of noise-removal steps, and the chosen noise schedule helps determine how that process unfolds. Some scheduling decisions remain heuristic. This paper develops a frequency-based analysis of inference to explain the relationship between the schedule and the spectral characteristics of the data.

Under a Gaussianity assumption, the authors express inference as a closed-form spectral transfer function. This describes how the generated signal evolves from the initial noise across spectral components. The formulation supplies a mathematical view of the synthesis process, making it possible to connect schedule structure with properties of the distribution being modeled.

The authors use this analysis to design noise schedules that depend on the data's spectral content. The resulting scheduling curves also provide theoretical justification for some existing practitioner heuristics. The Gaussianity assumption is central to the closed-form analysis, so its explanatory claims belong to that setting. The contribution gives schedule design a data-dependent theoretical basis and offers insight into the dynamics of diffusion inference.
neurips-2025-spectral-analysis-of-diffus.tldr: Under a Gaussianity assumption, a spectral analysis of diffusion inference yields data-dependent noise schedules and explains some scheduling heuristics.

paragraphs: Large covariance and kernel matrices can be too expensive to construct, yet their eigenvalue distributions are useful for quantities such as log-determinants and traces of matrix functions. Some estimation methods need only matrix-vector products. This paper studies a more restricted setting where even those operations are unavailable and access consists only of small submatrices.

The authors call these matrices impalpable because the full object cannot be directly accessed or applied as an operator. Their free decompression method draws on free probability theory to extrapolate from the empirical spectral densities of small submatrices. The target is the spectrum of the much larger matrix represented by those limited snapshots.

The paper evaluates the approach using synthetic examples with known limiting distributions from random matrix theory and real-world datasets whose full empirical eigenspectra can be used for comparison. These demonstrations support spectral estimation from restricted matrix access. The contribution addresses a distinct computational obstacle: obtaining useful spectral information when neither forming the matrix nor multiplying by it is feasible.
neurips-2025-spectral-estimation-with-fr.tldr: Free decompression estimates a large matrix's spectrum from small submatrices when full matrix access and matrix-vector products are unavailable.
